I own 200,000 domain names. I would like to create ai generated web sites with each one and get google to rank them as well as possible. How should I proceed?
Yes—but I would not start by automatically publishing 200,000 AI-generated sites. At that scale, the architecture and content strategy matter enormously.
Google explicitly says that using generative AI to create many pages without adding value can constitute “scaled content abuse.” It also lists “creating multiple sites with the intent of hiding the scaled nature of the content” as an example. AI itself isn't the problem; mass-produced, low-value content created primarily to rank is. https://t.co/iaFMVZJM7V
For a portfolio as large as yours, I would build a DomainMarket AI Publishing Platform and roll it out progressively.
1. Do not launch all 200,000 at once. Start with perhaps 500–1,000 of your domains. Divide them into cohorts by domain quality, commercial intent, subject matter, existing traffic/backlinks, and likelihood that the domain can support a genuinely useful website. Measure indexing, rankings, impressions, clicks, engagement and leads before expanding.
2. Give every domain a real purpose. The biggest mistake would be generating essentially the same five-page website 200,000 times. Instead, classify each domain with AI and assign it a site type appropriate to the name. For example:
https://t.co/qQnG8KDyC5 → birthday planning/content/tools
https://t.co/wMGLXUdHQo → local contractor resource
https://t.co/KaD7ZXOb8b → actual calculator + educational content
https://t.co/MCQBmpQMSS → watch information/database
https://t.co/rapnqBqZzb → training guides/tools
AI-related domain → specialized AI tool/resource
Google's current guidance emphasizes unique, non-commodity content rather than information that simply restates what already exists online.
3. Build functionality, not just articles. This is probably the most important opportunity. Have AI create useful things appropriate to each domain: calculators, comparison engines, directories, searchable databases, quizzes, checklists, generators, glossaries, statistics, interactive tools and original data presentations. A genuinely useful tool gives Google—and humans—a reason to prefer the site over another generic AI article.
4. Create an AI “site architect” before the AI writer. For every domain, your system should first determine what the phrase means, dominant search intent, likely audience, industry, commercial intent, relevant entities, appropriate site type, best information architecture, competing sites, opportunities competitors haven't covered, and what proprietary/useful feature can be added. Only after that should it generate pages.
5. Use a page-generation pipeline rather than one-shot prompts. I would structure it roughly as:
Domain → semantic analysis → search-intent research → competitor/SERP research → site strategy → keyword/topic map → page specifications → research/data gathering → content generation → fact verification → duplication check → quality scoring → internal linking → structured data → human/AI QA → publish.
6. Set a high publication threshold. AI should be allowed to reject its own work. Give every proposed page a score for originality, usefulness, factual reliability, search intent match, depth, duplication, readability and commercial value. For example, don't publish anything scoring below 85/100. This dramatically changes the economics: generating content is almost free, so you can afford to discard mediocre content.
7. Don't create hundreds of pages merely to capture keyword variations. Google specifically warns against creating separate content for every possible search variation or “fan-out query” primarily to manipulate rankings. Instead, one excellent comprehensive page should capture many related searches.
8. Leverage the domain itself intelligently. Your portfolio gives you an unusual advantage: many domains presumably describe exactly what someone is interested in. But I would not assume an exact-match domain alone will rank. Treat the domain as branding and topical positioning; the website still needs to earn rankings through usefulness, authority, links and user satisfaction.
9. Create legitimate authorship and ownership signals. Every site should clearly identify who operates it, why it exists, contact information, editorial standards, sources where appropriate, correction policy where appropriate, and how AI is being used where disclosure makes sense. Google's people-first guidance specifically discusses “Who, How, and Why,” including disclosure considerations when automation substantially generates content.
10. Use one common technology platform behind everything. You absolutely do not want to administer 200,000 WordPress installations. I'd use a centrally managed, API-driven publishing platform with reusable templates/components but domain-specific content and functionality. Something like Cloudflare/CDN + centralized application/database + automated SSL/DNS + programmatic site generation would make much more sense.
11. Keep the visual templates diverse where appropriate—but don't try to disguise common ownership. You can have perhaps 20–50 high-quality site frameworks selected according to industry and site type. The purpose of different templates should be creating the best UX for each subject, not making Google believe unrelated operators own the sites. Google's spam policy specifically warns about multiple sites used to conceal scaled content.
12. Build technical SEO into the platform. Automatically generate good titles/H1s, canonical URLs, crawlable navigation, breadcrumbs, appropriate https://t.co/oQLAwoouGn markup, OpenGraph data, robots.txt, XML sitemaps, image alt text, fast responsive pages and clean internal links. Google continues to recommend crawlable links, descriptive language, useful structured data and strong page experience. A sitemap is limited to 50,000 URLs, so larger individual properties require multiple sitemaps/sitemap indexes.
13. Don't overlook images and video. For valuable domains, create original diagrams, illustrations, charts and eventually video. Google's 2026 AI-search guidance specifically encourages useful images/video alongside unique textual content.
14. Build a proprietary-data layer. This could become your biggest SEO moat. Rather than having AI merely rewrite the Internet, obtain/licence/publicly source structured datasets and transform them into genuinely useful information. A real estate domain might have housing statistics; a travel domain could have destination data; a financial domain could have historical datasets and calculators. AI becomes the interface to unique information rather than the source of generic prose.
15. Monetize according to the domain. Don't force every domain into the same AdSense/affiliate model. Some should generate advertising revenue; others affiliate revenue, leads, subscriptions, SaaS/tool revenue or ecommerce opportunities. And importantly for your business, every developed site could still discreetly indicate that the domain/business may be available for acquisition.
16. Use https://t.co/3NBjGka1ZF as the portfolio's commercial backbone rather than building a giant SEO link network. Each developed property can have a legitimate “Domain inquiries” or “Acquire this domain/business” path to DomainMarket. I would avoid massive automated keyword-rich cross-linking among your 200,000 sites.
17. Measure everything centrally. Build one dashboard showing each domain's Google indexed pages, impressions, average position, clicks, CTR, referring domains, traffic, engagement, conversions/leads, revenue, content-production cost and domain-sale inquiries. Then calculate an internal SEO Opportunity Score and automatically direct additional content investment toward winners.
18. Let the winners compound. Suppose you launch 1,000. Perhaps 600 do essentially nothing, 250 get modest impressions, 100 begin getting meaningful traffic and 50 show unusually strong traction. Stop spending resources on the 600 and dramatically improve the 50 winners. Add original research, tools, data, editorial review and link acquisition to those properties.
19. Then repeat. 1,000 domains → measure → learn → improve system → next 5,000 → measure → next 10,000. Eventually you could have a sophisticated system evaluating all 200,000 domains, while only publishing sites where your models predict sufficient opportunity.
20. Optimize for Google AI Mode/AI Overviews as well as conventional results. This is increasingly important. Google's May 2026 guidance says traditional SEO fundamentals still apply to its generative AI search experiences and emphasizes unique, valuable, expert-led/non-commodity material rather than special “GEO hacks.”
The key conceptual change I would make to your original idea is:
Don't build 200,000 AI-generated websites. Build an AI system capable of developing 200,000 domains into useful Internet properties—and let data determine which ones deserve development.
With your portfolio size, this could actually be more interesting than a conventional SEO project. You have enough domains to run statistically meaningful experiments: 100 different site structures, content strategies, page depths, tool types and monetization approaches, then continuously allocate resources toward whatever Google and users respond to.
If I were implementing this for DomainMarket, my first target would be 1,000 domains, roughly 20–30 site archetypes, a centralized AI content/QA system, automated technical SEO, Search Console data ingestion, and an automated scoring dashboard. After 60–90 days, we'd know vastly more about which approach is worth scaling to the other 199,000 domains. Google's own guidance is particularly relevant here because merely being technically compliant doesn't guarantee crawling, indexing, or visibility.
I can also design the actual technical architecture and AI workflow for doing this at 200,000-domain scale—including hosting architecture, AI models/prompts, estimated generation/hosting costs, automated Google/Search Console setup, templates, database structure, and how I'd select the first 1,000 domains from your DomainMarket inventory. That would be the logical next step.
Google Search's guidance on using generative AI content on your website
Generative AI can be particularly useful when researching a topic, and to add structure to original content. However, using generative AI tools or other similar tools to generate many pages without adding value for users may violate Google's spam policy on scaled content abuse. If you're using generative AI content on your website, make sure your work meets the standards of the Search Essentials and our spam policies.
You might find value in looking at the Search Quality Raters guidelines on how to evaluate both scaled content abuse (section 4.6.5) and main content created with little to no effort, little to no originality, and little to no added value (section 4.6.6). These guidelines are not a guide to ranking first in Google; they're used by our search raters to help evaluate the performance of our various search ranking systems, and their ratings don't directly influence ranking.
Focus on accuracy, quality, and relevance
When creating content for the web, focus on accuracy, quality, and relevance, especially when automatically generating the content. This includes metadata like <title> elements, meta description elements, structured data, and alternate texts for images, which can appear in Search results.
For structured data, also ensure compliance with the general guidelines, the specific policies for the individual search features, and validate the markup to ensure eligibility for Search features.
Give users context
Sharing information about how a piece of content was created can help give your readers more context. If you're automatically generating content, consider adding information on how your content was created in a way that makes sense for your audience, such as by providing more background information on how automation was used and adding image metadata.
For ecommerce sites, Google Merchant Center has policies for AI-generated content. In particular, AI-generated images must contain metadata using the IPTC DigitalSourceType TrainedAlgorithmicMedia metadata. AI-generated product data such as title and description attributes must be specified separately and labeled as AI-generated.
For more, see our FAQs in our blog post on AI-generated content.

Generative language modeling for antibody CDR grafting and alignment-driven de novo design

1. The paper introduces GenCDR, a framework-first autoregressive (LLaMA-style) antibody language model: it reads all framework regions (FR1–FR4) as the prompt, then generates all CDRs jointly as a variable-length response, creating a clean prompt–response boundary for reward attribution and alignment.

2. This re-ordering directly targets the core de novo antibody problem as an infilling task: CDR design conditioned on a fixed scaffold. Unlike left-to-right decoding (where early CDRs lack downstream framework context), GenCDR generates CDRs with full framework context available from the start.

3. GenCDR is presented as a model family covering common design settings: IgGenCDR (unpaired human OAS, ~254M sequences), p-IgGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~1.8M natively paired VH–VL sequences), and NanoGenCDR (fine-tuned on ~6.5M camelid VHH from INDI plus human OAS heavy chains in a 1:1 mixture to preserve humanness on humanized scaffolds).

4. On CDR recovery (next-token prediction accuracy over CDR tokens) using a CDR3-disjoint held-out test set designed to reduce leakage, framework-first ordering improves over a same-sized left-to-right ablation and surpasses prior autoregressive baselines (including p-IgGen, ProGen2-OAS, and IgLM) across essentially all loops, with especially strong gains where downstream context matters most (e.g., CDR1).

5. De novo generation quality: when prompted with held-out frameworks and sampling CDRs jointly, GenCDR reproduces natural CDR length distributions closely (across all loops), while maintaining human-likeness (OASis), naturalness (ESM-2 PLL), and diversity/novelty with smooth trade-offs across sampling temperatures.

6. A key design consequence of the framework-first factorization is separable CDR likelihoods: GenCDR can score only the generated CDR block (rather than conflating framework+CDR likelihood), enabling clearer optimization targets and more principled alignment for CDR-centric objectives.

7. Likelihoods retain useful biological signal: GenCDR log-likelihood correlates zero-shot with experimental fitness/developability benchmarks (FLAb). The analysis also highlights assay locality: immunogenicity appears more CDR-driven, while expression is more framework-driven, and paired scoring (p-IgGenCDR) improves correlations when heavy+light are scored jointly.

8. NanoGenCDR extends the framework-first approach to nanobodies: fine-tuning closes the human→camelid distribution shift in CDR recovery, generates plausible/developable VHHs (including fold-confidence and developability flag rates comparable to reference), and improves humanness on humanized VHH scaffolds specifically due to the camelid+human mixture strategy.

9. Alignment-driven de novo design: the prompt–response boundary enables iterative alignment with weighted DPO (wDPO) using rewards computed only on the generated CDR completion. They optimize a composite reward from antibody–antigen co-folding metrics (Boltz-2) plus non-differentiable developability liability rules, demonstrating multi-objective steering without explicit antigen encoding in the model input.

10. In a PD-L1 nanobody design benchmark, four rounds of alignment drive near-perfect compliance with length/liability constraints after one round (acceptance ~23.8% → ~99.8–100%), and achieve in silico interface metrics competitive with a structure-conditioned diffusion pipeline (BoltzGen) at roughly half the sampling budget, while producing sequences that remain more “natural” under independent language-model scoring—suggesting KL-anchored alignment can push target-facing metrics without excessive distributional drift.

Apparently people are also angry that I posted about Luma and played around with AI recently...

So again:

1) Luma was a nice little hobby thing on the side. Wicked is my main gig, obviously! Luma is a project I had in mind for almost a decade, built 2 prototypes of it already over the years (it's the project I showed to Oculus back in 2016 or so) and then did a gamejam where I finally solved the issues I got stuck on before.

It was the first game I was able to make with my 8 year old son. He and I played Minecraft together a lot and we talked about how one could make an even better game and that's how Luma jumped back into my mind.

And honestly, it was delightful to be able to make something with him. As a parent, it's amazing if you find something that you and your kid both get excited about. Him coming home from school with dozens of ideas and overflowing with creative energy was one of the best moments for me this year.

So, sue me if you get offended that I spent a bunch of time with my son being creative together. I posted about it online because it's just a genuinely good game already!

Here try it yourself: https://t.co/Xu3yzKOs8p
It's really good! 👍

2) I already made my stance on AI clear. No, we're not using any generative AI stuff on Wicked and people who now claim otherwise are just making shit up in a ridiculous fashion. AI at this stage isn't good enough to create assets or any such thing, not at the quality standards we require at Moon. Any good gamedev knows what AI can do and what it can't. And if they don't, they're not taking their jobs seriously.

But of course we're using AI to help with tooling, bugfixes and so on, like everyone else is. We'd be stupid not to. It's a genuinely useful tool.

3) A similar thing happened with https://t.co/JolbgwKsO7 - It's a database I built for myself and for our team to keep track of things early on. But then it became clear that most gamers would get a huge kick out of it, so I released it.

And since then, I got tons and tons and tons of messages from industry folks and players that they're using it every day now. We had like 300k visitors on the site now and people are daily driving it to help them find new games.

What is there to get outraged about? How about we let people have fun and celebrate if they have a good time?

The internet can be exhausting these days...

Apparently I’m a “gooner” now because I posted some AI cowboy art featuring attractive men.

Excellent. Add it to my qualifications.

Although, if depicting or appreciating the human body makes someone a gooner, we’re going to need to make some fairly substantial revisions to the history of art.

The ancient Greeks might need to explain all those exquisitely proportioned naked athletes they carved in marble. Michelangelo is going to have an absolutely dreadful meeting with HR over David. Botticelli put Venus naked on a shell and somehow Western civilisation staggered onward. Rubens painted flesh with glorious enthusiasm. Bernini turned marble into bodies so tactile they appear to yield beneath fingertips. Rodin gave us The Kiss. Renaissance painters filled churches and palaces with muscular saints, exposed breasts, beautiful bodies and enough strategically placed fabric to keep art historians employed for centuries.

Then came photography. Cinema. Fashion illustration. Pulp covers. Pin-ups. Comics. Album covers. Digital painting. Fantasy art. Video games. CGI. And now generative art.

The medium changes. Human fascination with beauty, bodies, sensuality, masculinity and femininity does not.

But apparently an adult woman posts a handsome cowboy in 2026 and suddenly some  human on X becomes the Pornography Constable.

It’s particularly funny because reducing every depiction of an attractive human body to masturbation says considerably more about the person doing the reducing than it does about the artist.

Sometimes art is profound. Sometimes it is political. Sometimes it explores sexuality. Sometimes it exists because something is beautiful, strange, funny, provocative or aesthetically delicious.

And sometimes I make hot fucking cowboys because I can.

Art survived the naked Greeks.

I suspect it will survive my cowboys. 🤠

The guy who helped ship ChatGPT just said that same paradigm is why AI still can't automate real work.

Diogo Almeida spent years at OpenAI building the human-feedback techniques behind InstructGPT and ChatGPT. 

He left in 2024 to start TypeSafe AI. They just shipped their first product: a new model class called System One Models, and its first public model, Jev.

His bet: LLMs are trained on human preference and generate strings one token at a time. Great for chat. 

Bad for software, strings have to be parsed and validated before code can trust them, and there's always a chance the model goes off the rails.

Jev drops strings entirely.

→ Outputs typed, structured values instead of text — the schema is defined in advance, so type errors are mathematically impossible
→ Generates every output in parallel instead of token-by-token, so there's nothing to hallucinate into
→ Runs end-to-end in 70-500ms vs. 3-329 seconds for frontier LLMs
→ Costs $0.042 per million input tokens, output is free
→ Trained with a new method they call RLCD- optimized for calibrated probabilities on decisions, not for what a human rater would approve of

This isn't a ChatGPT competitor. It's not built for conversation at all. It's built to sit inside software and make the thousands of small, fuzzy decisions (classify, route, score, extract) that current LLMs are too slow, too expensive, and too unpredictable to run at scale.
